_comment: directoryOrder exists for dependency ordering, and it is now load-bearing rather than
precautionary. The nine type tables are mutually independent — no seeded row in one references a
row in another — but PIPELINES ARE SEEDED NOW, and they depend on four of them: Pipeline resolves
DealType and ForecastCategoryType, PipelineStage resolves DealStatusType and
ForecastCategoryType, and pipeline-stages resolves its PipelineID out of pipelines. Get that order
wrong and the push fails on an unresolvable lookup — see bizapps-orders, where exactly that
mistake halted a push at 14 of 23 directories and left nine directories of metadata unpushed for
days (bizapps-sales docs/KNOWN-ISSUES.md KI-22).
THIS FILE USED TO SAY PIPELINES ARE NOT SEEDED HERE, and the reasoning was sound while it lasted:
a pipeline is per-deployment data, not vocabulary. What changed is the process, not the taxonomy.
'Install the app and test it' is now the dev->test workflow, and an app that installs with no
pipeline is one where nobody can create a deal or render a board column — the type tables are all
present and the app is still unusable. A default a deployment does not want is cheaper to change
than a blocker it did not expect, so the pair the demo script already describes ships as metadata:
B2B (Discovery, Qualification, Proposal, Negotiation, Signed, Lost) and D2C (Introduced,
Evaluating, Booked), with OrderStatusOnEntry populated per D-OS1.
The company is the part that made this awkward and is worth reading before changing it: see
pipelines/.mj-sync.json. Pipeline.CompanyID is NOT NULL (D5) and companies are MJ core data, so
the seed resolves 'Default Company' and relies on this file's autoCreateMissingRecords to create
it on a bare install. scripts/seed-dev-data.sh repoints the two rows at the local dev companies,
so a development host gets these pipelines on real companies rather than a second set of them.
DealType.DefaultPipelineID is STILL deliberately left NULL. It is the other half of the DealType
<-> Pipeline cycle, and now that pipelines exist it could be filled — but a default pipeline per
deal type is a routing decision a deployment should make, and nothing in the app requires it.
_comment_remote_operations: remote-operation-categories MUST precede remote-operations: the operation rows resolve their
CategoryID with @lookup against a category by Name, so the category has to exist first. This is
the first entry in this list where the ordering is genuinely load-bearing rather than
precautionary — get it wrong and the push fails on an unresolvable lookup.
_comment_entity_relationships: entity-relationships is the odd one out: it does not seed rows at all. It fills in one column on
three EntityRelationship rows CodeGen already created, turning them into typed writable child
collections on Deal. It is listed last because it depends on nothing, and because reading it last
matches when it matters — CodeGen pass 2 is what consumes it. See its README.
